articles.excerpt: GraphSloth: auditing 29 abandoned project folders so I don't have to Live demo · Source My ~/Desktop/Project folder has 29 project folders in it, about 95GB total. I had no idea which ones were safe t…
articles.body: GraphSloth: auditing 29 abandoned project folders so I don't have to Live demo · Source What I Built My ~/Desktop/Project folder has 29 project folders in it, about 95GB total. I had no idea which ones were safe to archive and which ones I'd regret deleting. Auditing that by hand is exactly the kind of task International Sloth Day exists for, so I built something to do it instead. GraphSloth scans a folder of projects and, for each one, pulls real facts: disk size, git commit age, and (for git repos) a real Graphify structural extraction — real tree-sitter AST parsing, zero LLM cost — giving node/edge counts and the most-referenced symbol.

articles.title: Why compliance teams are banning AI meeting assistants: A guide to hidden privacy risks in 2026
articles.excerpt: 1. The EU AI Act Has Turned Meeting Privacy Into a Legal Deadline €15 million or 3% of worldwide revenue. That's the exposure the EU AI Act created for organizations whose meeting assistants record ca…
articles.body: 1. The EU AI Act Has Turned Meeting Privacy Into a Legal Deadline €15 million or 3% of worldwide revenue. That's the exposure the EU AI Act created for organizations whose meeting assistants record calls without demonstrable disclosure — and it became enforceable on August 2, 2026. The tools aren't the problem. One design choice is: a bot that joins the call as a participant and sends the audio to a third-party server. Compliance teams are banning that architecture, not AI itself. 2. Three Capture Models — and Why the Difference Is Legal, Not Cosmetic A meeting bot does not just listen. It receives the same audio stream the platform sends to human attendees. Then it sends that stream to infrastructure the meeting host does not control. Not all assistants work this way.

articles.title: Git Is Not a Backup: Cloud Backup vs Local Backup for Developers
articles.excerpt: A few years ago I would have told you my code was "backed up" because it was on GitHub. Then I started thinking about everything that isn't in the repo: the .env files, the local database, the client…
articles.body: A few years ago I would have told you my code was "backed up" because it was on GitHub. Then I started thinking about everything that isn't in the repo: the .env files, the local database, the client assets, the notes, and the config that only exists on my laptop. If you freelance, run a small agency, or look after IT for a small business, the cloud backup vs. local backup question is worth ten minutes of your time. Here's a developer-friendly way to think about it, plus a setup you can copy. First, a myth: Git is not a backup Git is great at history and collaboration. It is a poor backup for the whole machine because: Untracked and ignored files ( .env , local databases, and build artefacts you can't regenerate) aren't in it. A force-push or deleted remote can wipe history.

articles.title: The 6 native categories of the guardrail
articles.excerpt: Short answer The six native categories of IBM’s Granite guardrails are: harmful content, privacy, bias and fairness, robustness, transparency, and accountability. These categories structure the model’…
articles.body: Short answer The six native categories of IBM’s Granite guardrails are: harmful content , privacy , bias and fairness , robustness , transparency , and accountability . These categories structure the model’s built-in safety controls to align with enterprise AI governance standards. TL;DR Granite guardrails are pre-configured, domain-agnostic safety layers embedded in IBM’s foundation models. All six categories are implemented at inference time via runtime policy enforcement—not just post-hoc filtering. “Harmful content” covers violence, hate, self-harm, and illegal acts; “privacy” enforces PII redaction and data minimization. “Bias and fairness” includes demographic parity checks across protected attributes (e.g., gender, ethnicity) per NIST AI RMF guidance.

articles.title: Ludo game vs Parchís: Spain's cousin, with a five to leave the nest
articles.excerpt: Put a Ludo board next to a Parchís board and you could take them for twins. Both are cross-shaped, both have four colours and four pieces per player, and both are played with one die. Parchís is the S…
articles.body: Put a Ludo board next to a Parchís board and you could take them for twins. Both are cross-shaped, both have four colours and four pieces per player, and both are played with one die. Parchís is the Spanish member of the family, and it is just different enough to be worth knowing. If you enjoy the Ludo game, here is how its Spanish cousin plays. Where does Parchís come from? Parchís is a Spanish adaptation of Pachisi, the Indian race game that Ludo also descends from. It is very popular in Spain, and it is also played in other parts of Europe and in northern Morocco. The standard board has 68 spaces. Boards for six players have 102, and for eight players 136. Which number frees a piece? In Ludo a six lets a piece out of base. In Parchís it is a five.

articles.excerpt: Rocket Lab launched a trio of private signals-intelligence satellites to orbit today (Oct. 21), the 19th mission of the year for the California-based company.
articles.body: Rocket Lab launched a trio of private signals-intelligence satellites to orbit today (Oct. 23). The mission lifted off aboard an Electron rocket from Rocket Lab’s New Zealand launch site today at 3:11 a.m. EDT (0711 GMT; 8:11 p.m. local time in New Zealand). The Electron carried three "Hawk" satellites for the Virginia-based company HawkEye 360, which explains the name Rocket Lab gave to the mission: "We're Not Hawking Around." If all goes according to plan, the three Hawks will be deployed into low Earth orbit (LEO), at an altitude of 323 miles (520 kilometers). Once up there and commissioned, the satellites will scan the globe for radio frequency (RF) emissions.

articles.title: Space debris: Are we on track for true sustainability? (op-ed)
articles.excerpt: Space is a critical infrastructure layer, underpinning nearly all systems that enable modern life as we know it. It’s therefore critical to maintain a safe and clean orbital environment.
articles.body: David Zamora is the chairman of the Space Data Association. He contributed this article to Space.com's Expert Voices: Op-Ed & Insights . The commercialization of space is well underway, and as a result, Earth’s orbit is becoming ever more congested. The current number of active satellites in orbit stands at around 16,000, according to the European Space Agency( ESA), and this number is expected to jump close to 60,000 by 2035, Novaspace projects . While it’s not always given the recognition it deserves, space has fast become a critical infrastructure layer, underpinning nearly all systems that enable modern life as we know it. Therefore, it’s critical that a safe and clean operating landscape is maintained.

articles.body: Pillow, the most widely used image library for Python, can be made to run operating system commands on a server by specifying the name of a file it is told to open. The flaw, CVE-2026-112900, is in the way Pillow handles EPS images, which it opens by passing the file's name to Ghostscript, a separate program it runs to turn the image into pixels, without checking the name first.

articles.body: Europe has dropped the ball on the prototype for its first reusable spacecraft. Or, rather, the prototype itself was dropped — on purpose — but the outcome of its fall was not what engineers had hoped for. The incident occurred during an Oct. 6 drop test of the full-scale Space Rider model , from the European Space Agency (ESA). The robotic vehicle's initial drogue parachute deployed successfully, but its main parafoil detached during deployment, leaving the prototype unable to slow its descent before crashing into the ground, according to ESA officials. The cause of the failure remains under investigation.

articles.body: Members of the media are invited to join NASA at the 2026 von Braun Space Exploration Symposium from Monday, Oct. 26, to Wednesday, Oct. 28, at the University of Alabama in Huntsville. This year’s symposium is focused on humanity’s return to the Moon, sustainable lunar infrastructure, advanced space propulsion, and the evolving space workforce. Panels include discussions on Artemis II and III, space propulsion flash talks, building utilities and infrastructure for sustainable lunar operations, Moon base supply chain resilience, space nuclear technology, navigating the new NASA workforce, and engineering the future, featuring keynotes and awards presentations.

articles.body: NASA, ESA, Michael Jones (California Institute of Technology); Image Processing: Gladys Kober (NASA/Catholic University of America) This NASA Hubble Space Telescope image released on Oct. 16, 2026, features the edge-on, intermediate spiral galaxy NGC 1827, located roughly 37 million light-years away in the constellation Columba, the Dove. Hubble captured the image as part of a survey looking at 260 satellite galaxies around 22 Milky Way-like host galaxies within a radius of about 32 million light-years from Earth. Low-mass galaxies like the ones in this Hubble observing program provide a way to test the predictions of cosmological models on small scales, which struggle to match observations.
